source_references.name: OWASP Top 10 for Agentic Applications
source_references.why_it_matters: Vendor-neutral consensus guidance now names agent behavior hijacking, tool misuse, identity abuse, agentic supply chain, cascading failures, and rogue behavior as distinct risks.

source_references.name: Agentic AI Threats and Mitigations
source_references.why_it_matters: Threat-model-based agentic AI guidance reinforces that autonomy, tools, delegation, and retrieved context require controls beyond classic LLM app hardening.

source_references.name: OWASP Top 10 for Model Context Protocol
source_references.why_it_matters: MCP-specific risks include token mismanagement, scope creep, tool poisoning, command execution, auth gaps, missing telemetry, shadow servers, and context over-sharing.

source_references.name: Model Context Protocol Authorization Specification (2026-07-28 current revision)
source_references.why_it_matters: Current public MCP 2026-07-28 revision. The current MCP authorization spec requires OAuth 2.1 style bearer-token handling, resource indicators, token audience validation, PKCE, HTTPS, and strict token use.

source_references.name: Model Context Protocol Authorization Specification
source_references.why_it_matters: Prior MCP 2025-11-25 authorization revision kept as a historical source ID. Prefer the 2026-07-28 resource-indicator, audience, PKCE, and token-passthrough rules.

source_references.name: Model Context Protocol Security Best Practices (2026-07-28 current revision)
source_references.why_it_matters: Current MCP 2026-07-28 security guidance replaces session-hijacking assumptions with state-handle binding, forbids token passthrough, requires confused-deputy consent on proxies, and tightens SSRF controls during metadata and Client ID Metadata Document fetches.

source_references.name: Model Context Protocol Security Best Practices (2025-06-18 prior revision)
source_references.why_it_matters: Prior MCP security-best-practices revision kept as a historical source ID. Session-hijacking guidance applies only to 2025-11-25 and earlier protocol versions; prefer the 2026-07-28 state-handle controls.

source_references.name: Defend against indirect prompt injection attacks
source_references.why_it_matters: Microsoft frames indirect prompt injection as a defense-in-depth problem requiring prompt shields, spotlighting, plan drift detection, critic agents, tool-chain analysis, IFC, least privilege, short-lived privileges, and human review.

source_references.name: Understanding prompt injections: a frontier security challenge
source_references.why_it_matters: OpenAI describes prompt injection as a frontier social-engineering risk that grows as agents gain access to sensitive data and actions.

source_references.name: Safety in building agents
source_references.why_it_matters: Agent Builder guidance recommends structured outputs, clear developer guidance, tool approvals, guardrails, trace graders, evals, and careful MCP tool calling.

source_references.name: Designing AI agents to resist prompt injection
source_references.why_it_matters: OpenAI notes that real prompt injection increasingly resembles social engineering, so defenses cannot depend only on string filtering.

source_references.name: NIST AI Risk Management Framework
source_references.why_it_matters: NIST continues expanding AI RMF work, including a 2026 concept note for trustworthy AI in critical infrastructure, reinforcing governance, measurement, and lifecycle risk management.

source_references.name: SI Agent Standards Initiative
source_references.why_it_matters: NIST is explicitly prioritizing interoperable agent standards, community-led protocols, agent authentication, identity infrastructure, and security evaluations for multi-agent systems.

source_references.name: CAISI Request for Information on Securing AI Agent Systems
source_references.why_it_matters: CAISI highlights risks from model outputs combined with software functionality, including indirect prompt injection, data poisoning, misaligned actions, and the need to constrain and monitor deployment access.

source_references.name: Back to the Future: Why Agentic AI Needs a Strong Identity Foundation
source_references.why_it_matters: NIST warns that agent rollouts are repeating IAM mistakes: shared human credentials, long-lived API keys and bearer tokens, overly broad access, local user-account impersonation, and over-reliance on human-in-the-loop approvals. Agents need unique identifiers and short-lived scoped credentials, not borrowed user sessions.

source_references.name: Summary of Comments on the Concept Paper (NCCoE Software and SI Agent Identity and Authorization)
source_references.why_it_matters: NCCoE's September 29, 2026 comments summary, drawn from more than 600 responses, says agent identity should reuse OAuth, SPIFFE, and MCP rather than a parallel stack, issue distinct verifiable non-human identities at ephemeral scale, and treat credential sharing and local user impersonation as anti-patterns.

source_references.name: Design Tenets for Agent Identity Management Systems
source_references.why_it_matters: NIST's October 27, 2026 design tenets, drawn from NCCoE comments and stakeholder engagement, require cryptographically verifiable identities distinct from humans and service accounts, attenuated sub-agent delegation, zero standing privilege, short-lived audience-specific grants, signed mandate statements, architectural separation of policy from reasoning, deterministic access decisions, consent-fatigue-aware HITL thresholds, continuous monitoring, and independent append-only evidence.

source_references.name: Artificial Intelligence Risk Management Framework: Generative Artificial Intelligence Profile
source_references.why_it_matters: The generative AI profile anchors data provenance, third-party, monitoring, evaluation, and risk-management expectations for enterprise AI systems.

source_references.name: AI Data Security: Best Practices for Securing Data Used to Train and Operate AI Systems
source_references.publisher: CISA, NSA, FBI, and international partners
source_references.why_it_matters: Joint guidance highlights data security, integrity, monitoring, threat detection, and network defense across AI development, testing, deployment, and operation.

source_references.name: Software Must Be Secure by Design, and Artificial Intelligence Is No Exception
source_references.why_it_matters: CISA argues that AI is software and should inherit secure-by-design defaults, lifecycle security, transparency, vulnerability handling, SBOM-style accountability, and privacy by default.

source_references.name: Securing the Agentic AI Control Plane: Announcing the MCP Security Resource Center
source_references.why_it_matters: CSA frames MCP as part of the agentic AI control plane and highlights rapid adoption, broad client/server growth, and the need for structured MCP security resources.

source_references.name: Agentic AI, MCP, and the Identity Explosion You Cannot Ignore
source_references.why_it_matters: Agentic AI creates non-human identity pressure because agents act through credentials, tokens, scopes, and delegated authority that traditional IAM often does not govern cleanly.

source_references.name: Capabilities-Based Risk Assessment for Agentic AI
source_references.why_it_matters: CSA's CBRA framing gives enterprises a consequence-driven way to measure autonomous AI risk through system criticality, AI autonomy, access permissions, and impact radius.

source_references.name: A2A Enterprise Implementation Guidance
source_references.why_it_matters: A2A treats remote agents as opaque HTTP services and emphasizes TLS, HTTP-layer authentication, skill-based authorization, data minimization, tracing, auditing, and API management.

source_references.name: A2A Protocol production-ready adoption milestone
source_references.why_it_matters: A2A moved into production-ready use with signed Agent Cards, multi-tenant security flows, cloud integrations, and a complementary split with MCP between agent coordination and tool access.

source_references.name: Key Practices for Incident Readiness and Response in Super Intelligence Training and Evaluation
source_references.why_it_matters: NIST CAISSI, NSA SISC, and CISA's October 16, 2026 practices (PP-26-4396 Ver 1.0) require that SI agents cannot access or interfere with monitoring processes and logs (§3.3) and that monitors, logging, egress allowlists, and shutdown mechanisms are verified before resuming agent activity (§7.3).

source_references.name: Careful Adoption of Agentic AI Services
source_references.publisher: CISA, ASD's ACSC, NSA, Canadian Cyber Centre, NCSC-NZ, NCSC-UK
source_references.why_it_matters: May 1, 2026 joint guidance: expanded attack surface, privilege creep, behavioral misalignment and obscure event records; avoid broad or unrestricted access, start with low-risk non-sensitive use cases, and account for agentic AI in the security model and risk posture.

source_references.name: GenAI and Agentic AI Exploit Roundup Q3 2026
source_references.why_it_matters: OWASP's Q3 2026 roundup records the Deadbugz malicious-MCP distribution campaign as an active attempted supply-chain campaign using MCP server metadata manipulation, with no confirmed compromise, plus evaluation-agent boundary escapes and excess-permission blast-radius incidents.

source_references.name: Agent Control Standard (ACS)
source_references.why_it_matters: ACS, now part of the OWASP GenAI Security Project, defines how agent platforms expose middleware hooks so declarative safety policies can be enforced at runtime across frameworks.

threat_signals.title: MCP token audience, passthrough, and scope creep are control-plane risks
threat_signals.trend: MCP 2026-07-28 remains the current public revision. Servers MUST NOT accept tokens that were not issued for them, MUST NOT pass those tokens to downstream APIs, MUST bind multi-request state handles to the authenticated user instead of treating handle possession as authentication, MUST implement per-client consent on OAuth proxies, and MUST treat OAuth metadata and Client ID Metadata Document fetches as SSRF-sensitive.

control_objectives: Issue per-run or per-workflow non-human identities instead of sharing human or local user credentials.
Bind delegated scopes to workflow, agent class, owner, and run ID, and attenuate sub-agent and downstream scopes so they cannot claim more authority than the parent.
Require short-lived, audience-restricted credentials, zero standing privilege when idle, and runtime revocation.
Keep access decisions deterministic and architecturally separate from the reasoning model; require signed mandate statements for delegated intent.
Preserve human owner and reviewer linkage in audit evidence without treating HITL prompts as a substitute for unique agent identity.
Prefer existing OAuth, SPIFFE, and MCP identity mechanisms over a parallel agent identity stack, and keep the secure path the easy path so impersonation does not become the default.
threat_signals.enterprise_risk: Shared bot accounts, human-token borrowing, local user-account impersonation, weak owner links, and missing revocation paths make incidents hard to contain or explain, and they undermine non-repudiation when an agent acts without a distinct identity. Ephemeral sub-agents and shadow local agents amplify this unless persistent trust anchors are paired with short-lived scoped credentials. A buyer can still fail if a sub-agent keeps parent-wide scope, idle agents retain standing privilege, the reasoning model grants access, delegated intent has no signed mandate, or the agent can write its own logs.
threat_signals.roadmap_action: Build tenant-side identity issuance adapters for OIDC, SPIFFE/SPIRE, source hosts, and MCP gateways.

threat_signals.title: Agent identities are becoming a new non-human identity class
threat_signals.trend: NIST's August 27, 2026 identity guidance warns that agent rollouts are repeating IAM mistakes: shared human credentials, long-lived API keys and bearer tokens, overly broad access, local user-account impersonation, and over-reliance on human-in-the-loop approvals. NCCoE's September 29, 2026 comments summary, based on more than 600 responses, confirms an evolutionary path: reuse OAuth, SPIFFE, and MCP rather than a parallel identity stack; issue distinct verifiable non-human identities at ephemeral-agent scale; and treat local user-or-admin impersonation plus credential sharing as anti-patterns, especially for externally owned agents. NIST's October 27, 2026 design tenets, drawn from those comments and stakeholder engagement, add attenuated sub-agent delegation, zero standing privilege, signed mandates, and architectural separation of policy from reasoning; in our reading, unique short-lived credentials alone are not sufficient. The first NCCoE implementation use case is identity, authentication, and authorization of AI agents in the software development lifecycle.

threat_signals.title: Agentic audit telemetry is becoming mandatory evidence, not observability nice-to-have
threat_signals.trend: Guidance increasingly expects monitoring, evidence, traceability, and lifecycle measurement for deployed AI systems, especially when they touch critical or enterprise operations. NIST's October 27, 2026 immutable-evidence tenet requires an unbroken, tamper-evident, append-only chain of custody for agent identity, delegated intent, and resulting actions, with logging infrastructure independent of the agent. NIST CAISSI, NSA SISC, and CISA require that agents cannot access or interfere with monitoring processes and logs (§3.3) and that containment is verified before resume (§7.3).

control_objectives: Assign risk ratings to tools and operations.
Hold privileged or irreversible operations for explicit approval at defined risk thresholds, with enough context for the correct authority and without training operators into habitual clicks.
Make approval prompts structured and auditable, bind them to signed mandate statements, and do not treat HITL as a substitute for unique agent identity and scoped credentials.
Preserve reviewer separation of duties before merge or release.
threat_signals.enterprise_risk: An attacker can manipulate an agent into requesting approval for the wrong thing, hiding sensitive data in a tool call, or bypassing human review through a lower-risk path. Frequent unstructured prompts also train operators to click through, recreating MFA-fatigue failure modes. Without signed mandates and risk-threshold HITL, a high-impact action can proceed on a habitual click or on model-authored intent that no originator actually signed.
threat_signals.roadmap_action: Add typed approval receipts and approval-bypass replay tests to the MCP policy evaluator.

threat_signals.title: Human approval is shifting from UX prompt to policy-enforced control
threat_signals.trend: High-risk agent actions need confirmations, tool safeguards, clear policies, trace grading, and reviewable execution plans. NIST warns that over-reliance on human-in-the-loop approvals causes consent fatigue, so approval needs a typed policy surface rather than a free-text negotiation with the model. NCCoE's September 29, 2026 comments summary likewise calls for risk-based human review of high-impact actions only, so operators are not trained to click through unstructured prompts. NIST's October 27, 2026 design tenets require organizations to define risk thresholds that trigger HITL with enough context for the correct authority, account for consent fatigue in those flows, and carry cryptographically signed mandate statements so originator intent is verifiable downstream instead of reconstructed from a chat prompt.
